newsitem.title: USA: Farmers seek larger reform in U.S. estate taxes.
newsitem.headline: Farmers seek larger reform in U.S. estate taxes.

text.p: The largest U.S. farm group expressed gratitude Tuesday that Congress was ready to ease the estate tax burden but warned the "incremental" changes in them "would prolong the stress on aging farmers."
President Dean Kleckner of the American Farm Bureau Federation said the group would press for improvements in tax bills pending in the House and Senate.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich joined Kleckner at a news conference in saying there should be no estate tax. But, they said, it was unlikely to be eliminated this year.
"We're not going to quit until we finish and until we're able to abolish the death tax and create the right kind of environment for American families," said Gingrich, Georgia Republican.

During the news conference, Kleckner handed over to Gingrich and Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer, Texas Republican, some 23,000 letters from farmers asking for repeal or revisions in revisions in the estate tax.

On average, farm families make the same amount of money as other families, Kleckner said, and their largest asset is land. With little cash to spare, they often must sell all or part of their land to pay estate taxes even if they want to keep the farm in the family.
"The death taxes...would eat it up," Kleckner said, describing what would happen to his medium-sized Iowa farm because of the inflation-driven increase in land values.

Before the news conference with Gingrich and Archer, Kleckner told a telephone news conference that the Farm Bureau was "disappointed with the slow phase-in of the estate tax provisions" in the House and Senate bills.
It would take until 2007 under the Senate bill to get to a $1 million estate tax credit -- "which is a long time," he said.
"An increase in the estate tax exemption has been long overdue but both of the bills, with their incremental increases, would prolong the stress on aging farmers and their families," Kleckner said.
"We are hopeful of obtaining earlier phase-in of reforms in the final tax bill."
Archer said his committee's tax bill had a $1 million credit and allowed 24 years to pay the libability without interest.
The Senate credit would be on top of the standard $600,000 exemption before estate taxes are due. The Senate bill also allows a $1 million exemption if land is put under conservation easement.
